title: Visual Timetable Corner
strapline: The day made visible — so a child who can't hold the routine in their head can see it on the wall.
intent: Children who find spoken instructions slippery get a picture of the day they can point to, return to and rely on.
Children feel safer because what's coming is knowable — snack, then garden, then home — not a series of surprises.
Children build a sense of time and sequence: first, next, then, last, before lunch, after sleep.
Children gain independence — checking the board themselves rather than asking an adult 'what now?' twenty times.
Children practise transitions calmly, because the change was flagged before it arrived.
implementation: Photograph your own routine — real snack table, real cloakroom, real key people — rather than clip-art a child can't map onto their day.
Keep it at child height by the door where children naturally gather, not up on an adult noticeboard.
Move a marker, arrow or peg down the strip as the day unfolds, and refer to it out loud: 'we've done singing, look, now it's garden time.'
Flag the wobbles in advance — a visiting adult, no garden because of rain, a fire drill — by adding or swapping a card and talking it through.
Give a child who needs it their own small travelling version — a lanyard strip or a first/next card — that goes where they go.
Model checking the board yourself so it reads as 'this is how we all know what's happening', not 'this is the special board for one child'.
key_questions: What have we done already today — can you show me on the board?
How do you feel about the change to our day?
Which part of the day are you looking forward to?
Something's different today — shall we sort the cards so we know?

impact.text: Children anticipate familiar routines and show they know what comes next.
Children follow the room's rhythms and transitions with reminders, using the board as their cue.
Children separate from carers and settle into the day more easily when the shape of it is visible.
Children use positional and sequence language — first, next, before lunch, after sleep — in their own talk.
Children handle a change to the day with support because it was flagged before it arrived.

enhancements: A 'finished' pocket or velcro box where completed cards go, so the day visibly shrinks as it passes.
A now/next/then three-frame beside the full strip for children who find the whole day too much to hold.
A home-to-nursery photo card so a child arriving upset can see 'grown-up comes back after story time'.
A pause/change card the whole group learns to read for unexpected events — a fire drill, a visitor, a sudden downpour.
Children take turns being 'timetable keeper', moving the marker and announcing what's next.

playing_exploring: Children explore the board freely, matching cards to the real places and people they show.
Handling and re-ordering the cards themselves turns an adult tool into something children own.
active_learning: Predicting the day and being right builds the confidence to try the next transition without a fuss.
Children take responsibility for checking the board, then acting on it independently.
creating_thinking: Children link cause and sequence — this happened, so that comes next — the seed of planning.
They spot when the day doesn't match the board and reason about what changed.
